title: Stop Coaching the Average Agent
summary: Traditional contact center coaching is built around averages. Learn how AI and 100% conversation analysis can make agent coaching more personalized, precise, continuous, and human.
body_markdown:
Imagine a contact center discovers that agents are struggling with objections.


The response is familiar. Managers identify the problem, create refresher training, schedule a team session, and ask everyone to review the same material.


There's just one problem. Not everyone struggles with objections.


One agent may handle objections beautifully but routinely forget a required disclosure. Another may know the product inside and out but make customers work too hard to get an answer. Someone else may follow every process perfectly but struggle to show empathy when a customer is frustrated.


And one of the agents sitting through that objection training may actually be the person everyone else should be learning from. Traditional coaching often treats agents as a group because historically, that's what the data allowed us to do. That is beginning to change.


## **Sampling Created Average Coaching**


For decades, contact center coaching has been constrained by a very practical problem: managers simply couldn't listen to everything.


When a supervisor or QA team reviews a small sample of an agent's conversations, they have to draw conclusions from limited information. A few calls become a proxy for overall performance.


That makes broad coaching understandable.


If a pattern appears across the calls you review, you coach to the pattern. If a QA metric declines across the team, you address it with the team. If a compliance issue surfaces, everyone may get refresher training because it's safer than trying to determine exactly who needs it.


The problem isn't that managers don't want to personalize coaching. They haven't had enough information to do it consistently.


## **What Changes When You Can See Every Conversation?**


Analyzing 100% of conversations changes the starting point.


Instead of asking, **"What should we coach the team on?"** managers can start asking, **"What does this particular agent need from me?"**


That is a fundamentally different question.


One agent might need help navigating pricing objections. Another might need coaching around customer effort. Another may consistently miss a particular compliance requirement. A new agent may understand the product but struggle when conversations move outside the expected flow.


The coaching doesn't have to begin with the average behavior of the group. It can begin with the actual behavior of the individual.


## **AI Should Make Coaching More Human**


There's a strange assumption embedded in some conversations about AI and employee performance: that more technology inevitably means less human management.


It can mean exactly the opposite.


Think about how much supervisor time is currently spent finding the coaching opportunity in the first place. Managers listen to recordings, review QA forms, compare metrics, investigate escalations, and try to piece together what an agent needs help with.


AI can do more of that detection.


It can surface repeated behaviors across conversations. Identify where an agent consistently struggles. Highlight examples. Compare patterns over time. Show whether a behavior is improving.


That gives the manager more time for the part that actually requires a human being: **the coaching itself.** The technology finds the signal. The manager helps the person improve.


## **Personalization Shouldn't Only Focus on What's Wrong**


There's another opportunity here that may be even more interesting.


Most coaching systems are designed to find deficiencies. What did the agent miss? Where did they lose points? Which behavior needs correction?


But 100% conversation analysis can also reveal what someone does exceptionally well.


Maybe one agent consistently de-escalates frustrated customers faster than everyone else. Another is particularly effective at explaining a complicated policy. Another handles objections in a way that produces better outcomes without sounding scripted. Another creates unusually low customer effort.


Those aren't just high scores.


They're organizational knowledge.


Once you can identify those behaviors consistently, coaching can become a two-way system. Managers can help agents improve where they struggle while also capturing what their strongest performers do differently and teaching those behaviors to others.


The best agent on the team becomes more than a top performer. They become a source of insight.


## **The Score Isn't the Coaching**


This also requires changing how we think about QA.


A score can tell an agent that they received an 82. It doesn't necessarily tell them how to get to 90.


Effective coaching requires getting underneath the number. Which behaviors affected the score? Are they recurring or isolated? What does the agent do well? Where specifically could a different behavior produce a better outcome?


At MosaicVoice, this is one reason we see automated QA and coaching as closely connected. Evaluating conversations at scale creates a much richer picture of performance than a handful of manually selected calls.


The purpose isn't simply to generate more scores. It's to make those scores more useful.


## **Coaching Should Change as the Agent Changes**


Personalized coaching also creates the opportunity for something traditional training struggles to deliver: continuity.


Imagine an agent is working on reducing unnecessary customer effort.


A manager identifies the issue, reviews examples with the agent, agrees on a different approach, and sends them back to work. Historically, validating whether the coaching worked could require waiting for the next QA review or manually finding another set of calls.


With continuous conversation analysis, the feedback loop can become much tighter.


-


Did the behavior change?


-


Is it improving?


-


Does it occur only with certain call types?


-


Did fixing one behavior create another problem?


The coaching conversation can evolve alongside the agent instead of restarting every time another call happens to be reviewed.


## **Managers Need Different Information Than Executives**


This is also where the way performance information is presented matters.


An executive may need to know whether quality is improving across the contact center. A QA leader may need to identify systemic patterns. A supervisor needs something much more specific.


**Who needs my attention today, and why?**


That's a very different use of data.


The best coaching technology shouldn't bury a manager under dozens of metrics or require them to investigate every agent manually. It should help direct their attention toward the people and behaviors where their involvement can have the greatest impact.


Technology shouldn't create another management task. It should help managers manage.


## **The Goal Isn't Standardization**


Contact centers need standards. Compliance requirements must be met. Processes need to be followed. Customers deserve a consistent level of service.


But consistency doesn't require identical people.


Some agents are naturally empathetic. Some are extraordinary problem solvers. Some understand complex products exceptionally well. Some are great at sales. Some can calm a difficult conversation almost instantly.


The opportunity isn't to use AI to make every agent behave exactly the same.


It's to establish the outcomes and behaviors that matter, understand how each person performs against them, and help each agent get better from wherever they are starting.


That's a much more individual approach to performance. And, perhaps counterintuitively, AI is what can finally make it practical at scale.


## **The Bottom Line**


For years, contact centers have had to coach groups because they couldn't consistently understand individuals.


That limitation is disappearing.


When organizations can analyze every conversation, coaching no longer has to be based on a handful of calls, broad team averages, or the assumption that everyone needs the same training.


Managers can understand where each agent struggles. They can identify where each agent excels. They can see whether coaching actually changes behavior. And they can spend less time searching for problems and more time helping people improve.


AI shouldn't make coaching less human.


**It should make coaching more individual.**
